analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to examine the prevalence and frequency of atypical symptoms among patients with dengue infection and to ascertain demographic characteristics and concomitant diseases. The authors highlighted the need for understanding these unusual presentations due to their potential impact on affected individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a case series conducted in India, focusing on patients with dengue infection who exhibited atypical symptoms. The case descriptions provided detailed clinical profiles of patients, including their age, symptoms, and neurological findings.
analysis.methods: The methods involved detailed clinical evaluations, including neurological assessments and laboratory investigations to confirm dengue infection. The study also included MRI brain imaging to identify any neurological complications associated with dengue infection.
analysis.main_results: The case series described a 39-year-old male patient with high-grade fever, vomiting, headache, and altered sensorium. Laboratory findings confirmed the presence of antichikungunya IgM in serum and CSF, indicating a possible overlap with chikungunya virus infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as highlighting the complexity of diagnosing dengue infection due to overlapping symptoms with other arboviruses like chikungunya. They emphasized the importance of recognizing atypical presentations to improve clinical outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the need for enhanced diagnostic protocols and awareness of atypical symptoms in dengue infection to prevent misdiagnosis and ensure timely and appropriate treatment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its case series design, which may not provide robust statistical evidence. However, the detailed clinical descriptions and laboratory findings offer valuable insights into the atypical manifestations of dengue infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a case series of dengue infection in India, highlighting the prevalence of atypical symptoms such as altered sensorium and neurological findings. The authors emphasize the challenges in diagnosing dengue due to overlapping symptoms with other arboviruses like chikungunya. The findings suggest the importance of recognizing these unusual presentations to improve clinical management and surveillance. The study's limitations include its case series design, which may not provide strong statistical evidence, but the detailed clinical and laboratory data offer meaningful insights into the complexity of dengue infection. The results contribute to the understanding of dengue's varied clinical manifestations and the need for enhanced diagnostic approaches.

elements_zh.methods: 这些方法涉及详细的临床评估,包括神经学评估和实验室研究以确认登革热感染。该研究还包括 MRI 脑成像,以识别与登革热感染相关的任何神经并发症。
elements_zh.main_results: 该病例系列描述了一名 39 岁男性患者,患有高烧、呕吐、头痛和感觉改变。实验室结果证实血清和脑脊液中存在抗基孔肯雅 IgM,表明可能与基孔肯雅病毒感染重叠。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为强调了诊断登革热感染的复杂性,因为其症状与基孔肯雅热等其他虫媒病毒有重叠。他们强调了识别非典型表现以改善临床结果的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调需要加强诊断方案和对登革热感染非典型症状的认识,以防止误诊并确保及时和适当的 治疗。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到病例系列设计的限制,可能无法提供可靠的统计证据。然而,详细的临床描述和实验室检查结果为了解登革热感染的非典型表现提供了宝贵的见解。

news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Fiji + 16 more Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 14 August 2026) Format Situation Report Sources SPC WHO Posted 14 Aug 2026 Originally published 14 Aug 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 734.62 KB) HIGHLIGHTS • Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs). • During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Naoero, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Naoero (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1). • Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 545 dengue confirmed cases, 175 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific. • The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 9 050 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year. • In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu. • The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases. • Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation. • The Cook Islands officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 25 May 2026. • Tonga has officially declared the end of its dengue outbreak on 31 July 2026. • As of 14 August 2026: o The dengue outbreak remains ongoing in Shefa Province, Vanuatu, with dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) continuing to circulate. o Low levels of transmission are observed in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna. analysis.time: Published 14 August 2026; event period 1 January 2025–14 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs): American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Naoero, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu, New Caledonia, Shefa Province (Vanuatu), Wallis and Futuna.
analysis.event: Multicountry dengue outbreaks reported by SPC and WHO; ongoing transmission in several PICs as of 14 August 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths in 2025; 4,545 confirmed cases, 175 hospitalisations, and 3 deaths from 1 January–2 July 2026; 9,050 dengue-like illness cases reported via PSSS; DENV-1 and DENV-2 circulating; 94% of 2026 cases concentrated in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Outbreaks declared ended in Cook Islands (25 May 2026) and Tonga (31 July 2026); Shefa Province (Vanuatu) remains ongoing with DENV-1 circulation; low-level transmission persists in American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Vanuatu, and Wallis and Futuna; surveillance via PSSS; serotypes DENV-1 and DENV-2 confirmed.

analysis.brief_en: As of 14 August 2026, twelve dengue outbreaks have affected Pacific Island Countries and Areas since January 2025, with 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths recorded in 2025 and 4,545 cases, 175 hospitalisations, and 3 deaths reported from January to early July 2026. The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System has logged 9,050 dengue-like illness cases to date, a decline compared with the same period last year. Dengue serotypes 1 and 2 are circulating, with American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia accounting for 94% of 2026 cases. Outbreaks have been officially declared over in the Cook Islands and Tonga, while Shefa Province in Vanuatu remains active with DENV-1 transmission. Low-level transmission continues in several territories, underscoring the need for sustained surveillance and vector control.

news.title_zh: 太平洋地区的登革热:多国情况(截至 2026 年 8 月 14 日) - ReliefWeb
news.source_body_en: As of 14 August 2026, twelve dengue outbreaks have affected Pacific Island Countries and Areas since January 2025, with 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths recorded in 2025 and 4,545 cases, 175 hospitalisations, and 3 deaths reported from January to early July 2026. The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System has logged 9,050 dengue-like illness cases to date, a decline compared with the same period last year. Dengue serotypes 1 and 2 are circulating, with American Samoa, Cook Islands, Samoa, and New Caledonia accounting for 94% of 2026 cases. Outbreaks have been officially declared over in the Cook Islands and Tonga, while Shefa Province in Vanuatu remains active with DENV-1 transmission. Low-level transmission continues in several territories, underscoring the need for sustained surveillance and vector control.
news.content_zh: 截至2026年8月14日,自2025年1月以来,已有12起登革热暴发影响太平洋岛屿国家和地区,2025年记录了21,258例确诊病例和21例死亡,2026年1月至7月初报告了4,545例病例、175例住院治疗和3例死亡。太平洋综合症监测系统已记录迄今为止,已有9,050例登革热类疾病病例,与去年同期相比有所下降。登革热血清型 1 和 2 正在流行,美属萨摩亚、库克群岛、萨摩亚和新喀里多尼亚占 2026 例病例的 94%。暴发 已在库克群岛和汤加正式宣布结束,而瓦努阿图谢法省仍然活跃于 DENV-1 传播。低级别的 传播 在多个地区继续存在,强调了持续 监测 和 媒介 控制的必要性。

Pylori Norovirus Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) Prevention Antibiotics Immunizations Vaccines Respiratory Infections Community-Acquired Pneumonia Measles Influenza Sexually Transmitted Diseases HIV / AIDS HPV HSV PrEP Skin & Soft Tissue Diseases MRSA Zoonotic & Vector-Borne Diseases Lyme Disease ZIKA Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America| Antibiotics Deconstructed| Bench to Bedside With SIDP| Antimicrobial Stewardship| Hepatitis Advertisement News|Articles|July 22, 2026 Contagion Contagion, Spring 2026 Digital Edition Volume 11 Issue 1 The Potential for Antivirals in Dengue Prophylaxis and Treatment Author(s)Noah Rosenberg, MD A study found that the investigational antiviral mosnodenvir reduced dengue virus infection RNA levels and symptoms in a controlled setting, supporting its potential as a prophylactic option. Advertisement Dengue virus infection, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito and caused by 4 distinct serotypes (DENV- 1-4), has an expanding global incidence and geographic range1 with locally acquired cases to Europe and the United States.2 While its cases are often mild or asymptomatic, dengue has the potential to cause severe illness, including shock and capillary leak syndrome, in both dengue-naive individuals and those with prior infection. Two vaccines have received worldwide approval for the prevention and long-term protection against reinfection. CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia; Sanofi) is approved for use in certain endemic areas among those aged 9 to 45 years with confirmed prior dengue infection. However, it is not approved for travelers and is being discontinued due to low demand. TAK-003 (Qdenga; Takeda) is approved in many countries for both seropositive and seronegative people. Despite vaccine development and availability, there are no approved antiviral prophylaxis or treatments against dengue, especially in those who are nonimmune. Mosnodenvir is an orally administered small-molecule agent developed to target dengue viral replication. The drug inhibits the de novo formation of the NS4B-NS3 complex. NS4B is a transmembrane protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, which binds NS3 to enhance NS3 helicase activity and increase viral replication.3 Preclinical studies have shown serotype-independent antiviral activity through in vitro and in vivo models, and recent phase 1 trials have demonstrated an acceptable safety profile.4 This FIGURE represents the viral replication complex of Dengue virus and the target of mosnodenvir. The NS4B complex is ER (endoplasmic reticulum) bound.5 Durbin and colleagues conducted a phase 2a trial that assessed the antiviral activity and safety of mosnodenvir in healthy participants who received a challenge virus with a hypoattenuated strain of DENV-3.6 This was designed as a doubleblind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Vermont, with funding from Johnson & Johnson. Healthy adults aged 18 to 55 years with no prior dengue exposure or endemic travel were enrolled and assigned to mosnodenvir or placebo in a stepwise, dose-escalation design. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive a 200-mg loading dose of oral mosnodenvir or placebo for the 5 days prior to challenge, and received an inoculation of underattenuated DENV-3 on day 0. The participants were then enrolled 2:1 into a high-dose cohort to establish safety. Further participants were randomly assigned to a high (100 mg), medium (50 mg), or low (10 mg) dose vs placebo in a 3:3:1 ratio for maintenance from day 1 to day 21. Patients were then followed through day 85. Primary outcomes included a reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels, clinical symptoms of infection, serologic response, and safety. The trial was powered to 85% probability to detect a 30% difference in RNA load between groups. High-dose mosnodenvir was associated with a significant reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels compared with placebo, with a clear dose-dependent antiviral effect regarding reduction in RNA levels and dengue infection–related symptoms. Participants with undetectable viral RNA did not have any detectable neutralizing antibodies, suggesting that successful inhibition of viral replication may prevent the development of humoral immunity. Mosnodenvir was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events. Only 2 severe events were noted: infection with SARS-CoV-2, and severe elevation in lipase and glucose levels. Together, the findings support mosnodenvir as a promising antiviral for dengue prophylaxis against DENV-3 infection, especially at high doses. However, the small sample size, use of a hypoattenuated DENV-3 challenge strain, and controlled timing of exposure limit generalizability to real-world settings with unpredictable exposure and multiple circulating serotypes. There is further work to be done to study those who have already been infected, those living in endemic regions, and the timing of prophylaxis. Despite these encouraging early results, Johnson & Johnson has discontinued further development of mosnodenvir. 7 However, other dengue antiviral strategies remain in development, including agents that target antiviral replication by Novartis, which are undergoing a phase 2 trial.8 There is also a monoclonal antibody undergoing evaluation.9 These show promise for the future of prophylaxis and treatment for dengue virus in the seropositive and seronegative populations. Pylori Norovirus Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) Prevention Antibiotics Immunizations Vaccines Respiratory Infections Community-Acquired Pneumonia Measles Influenza Sexually Transmitted Diseases HIV / AIDS HPV HSV PrEP Skin & Soft Tissue Diseases MRSA Zoonotic & Vector-Borne Diseases Lyme Disease ZIKA Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America| Antibiotics Deconstructed| Bench to Bedside With SIDP| Antimicrobial Stewardship| Hepatitis Advertisement News|Articles|July 22, 2026 Contagion Contagion, Spring 2026 Digital Edition Volume 11 Issue 1 The Potential for Antivirals in Dengue Prophylaxis and Treatment Author(s)Noah Rosenberg, MD A study found that the investigational antiviral mosnodenvir reduced dengue virus infection RNA levels and symptoms in a controlled setting, supporting its potential as a prophylactic option. Advertisement Dengue virus infection, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito and caused by 4 distinct serotypes (DENV- 1-4), has an expanding global incidence and geographic range1 with locally acquired cases to Europe and the United States.2 While its cases are often mild or asymptomatic, dengue has the potential to cause severe illness, including shock and capillary leak syndrome, in both dengue-naive individuals and those with prior infection. Two vaccines have received worldwide approval for the prevention and long-term protection against reinfection. CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia; Sanofi) is approved for use in certain endemic areas among those aged 9 to 45 years with confirmed prior dengue infection. However, it is not approved for travelers and is being discontinued due to low demand. TAK-003 (Qdenga; Takeda) is approved in many countries for both seropositive and seronegative people. Despite vaccine development and availability, there are no approved antiviral prophylaxis or treatments against dengue, especially in those who are nonimmune. Mosnodenvir is an orally administered small-molecule agent developed to target dengue viral replication. The drug inhibits the de novo formation of the NS4B-NS3 complex. NS4B is a transmembrane protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, which binds NS3 to enhance NS3 helicase activity and increase viral replication.3 Preclinical studies have shown serotype-independent antiviral activity through in vitro and in vivo models, and recent phase 1 trials have demonstrated an acceptable safety profile.4 This FIGURE represents the viral replication complex of Dengue virus and the target of mosnodenvir. The NS4B complex is ER (endoplasmic reticulum) bound.5 Durbin and colleagues conducted a phase 2a trial that assessed the antiviral activity and safety of mosnodenvir in healthy participants who received a challenge virus with a hypoattenuated strain of DENV-3.6 This was designed as a doubleblind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Vermont, with funding from Johnson & Johnson. Healthy adults aged 18 to 55 years with no prior dengue exposure or endemic travel were enrolled and assigned to mosnodenvir or placebo in a stepwise, dose-escalation design. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive a 200-mg loading dose of oral mosnodenvir or placebo for the 5 days prior to challenge, and received an inoculation of underattenuated DENV-3 on day 0. The participants were then enrolled 2:1 into a high-dose cohort to establish safety. Further participants were randomly assigned to a high (100 mg), medium (50 mg), or low (10 mg) dose vs placebo in a 3:3:1 ratio for maintenance from day 1 to day 21. Patients were then followed through day 85. Primary outcomes included a reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels, clinical symptoms of infection, serologic response, and safety. The trial was powered to 85% probability to detect a 30% difference in RNA load between groups. High-dose mosnodenvir was associated with a significant reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels compared with placebo, with a clear dose-dependent antiviral effect regarding reduction in RNA levels and dengue infection–related symptoms. Participants with undetectable viral RNA did not have any detectable neutralizing antibodies, suggesting that successful inhibition of viral replication may prevent the development of humoral immunity. Mosnodenvir was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events. Only 2 severe events were noted: infection with SARS-CoV-2, and severe elevation in lipase and glucose levels. Together, the findings support mosnodenvir as a promising antiviral for dengue prophylaxis against DENV-3 infection, especially at high doses. However, the small sample size, use of a hypoattenuated DENV-3 challenge strain, and controlled timing of exposure limit generalizability to real-world settings with unpredictable exposure and multiple circulating serotypes. There is further work to be done to study those who have already been infected, those living in endemic regions, and the timing of prophylaxis. Despite these encouraging early results, Johnson & Johnson has discontinued further development of mosnodenvir. 7 However, other dengue antiviral strategies remain in development, including agents that target antiviral replication by Novartis, which are undergoing a phase 2 trial.8 There is also a monoclonal antibody undergoing evaluation.9 These show promise for the future of prophylaxis and treatment for dengue virus in the seropositive and seronegative populations. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-17; event described as a phase 2a trial conducted in 2025 and reported in 2025–2026 literature.
analysis.location_and_population: United States (Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; University of Vermont, Burlington, VT); healthy adults aged 18–55 years with no prior dengue exposure or endemic travel.
analysis.event: A phase 2a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated the investigational antiviral mosnodenvir for dengue prophylaxis; results showed dose-dependent reductions in DENV-3 RNA levels and dengue-related symptoms, supporting potential prophylactic use. Reported by Durbin et al. in the New England Journal of Medicine.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No clinical cases or deaths reported in the trial; small sample size (healthy volunteers) limits population-level impact assessment. Mosnodenvir generally well tolerated; two severe adverse events (SARS-CoV-2 infection; elevated lipase and glucose) were reported. Dengue globally expanding with locally acquired cases in Europe and the United States.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Investigation ongoing; phase 2a trial completed with promising early results. Generalizability limited by small sample, use of hypoattenuated DENV-3 challenge, and controlled exposure timing. Further studies needed in endemic regions, seropositive individuals, and real-world exposure scenarios. Johnson & Johnson discontinued further development of mosnodenvir despite encouraging results.

analysis.brief_en: A phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that the oral antiviral mosnodenvir significantly reduced DENV-3 RNA levels and dengue-related symptoms in healthy adults exposed to a controlled hypoattenuated dengue challenge, demonstrating a dose-dependent prophylactic effect. Conducted in the United States with 18–55-year-old volunteers without prior dengue exposure, the study reported mosnodenvir was generally well tolerated, though two severe adverse events occurred. Despite these encouraging early results, the drug’s developer has discontinued further development. The findings underscore the unmet need for dengue antivirals amid expanding global transmission, including locally acquired cases in Europe and the United States, where no approved antiviral prophylaxis or treatments currently exist.

[ Photo by PAWICH SATTALERD ] Pinellas County reports two cases of dengue, first in 15 years Dengue is a viral infection spread by mosquito bites. Symptoms include fever, severe headache and joint pain. By Mia Taubenblat Yesterday The Florida Department of Health reported two cases of mosquito-borne dengue in Pinellas County on Aug. 12. Dengue fever is a viral illness transmitted through the bite of aedes aegypti and aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which are both found in Florida. Symptoms of dengue include severe muscle aches, joint pain, fever, nausea, pain behind the eyes, vomiting and rash. They typically present within 15 days of an infected mosquito bite. Pinellas County hasn’t reported a case of locally-acquired dengue in over 15 years, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It is unclear if the new cases were identified in Palm Harbor, but health officials are focusing their surveillance in that area. The Hillsborough health department also issued a mosquito-borne illness alert Aug. 12, announcing an eighth case of dengue in the county. There is no specific treatment for dengue. Rest, drinking fluids and easing symptoms with acetaminophen are recommended. Tampa Bay residents presenting symptoms should see a healthcare provider and contact the health department. Going door-to-door on Pinellas residents’ private property, where mosquitoes are most commonly found, will be the priority of Pinellas County Mosquito Control’s dengue prevention efforts. Mosquito control will conduct daytime backpack fogging treatments and door-to-door inspections in Palm Harbor. The inspections aim to reduce areas where mosquitoes breed, such as standing water in animal dishes, flower pots and buckets. Following the cases, mosquito control is advising Palm Harbor residents to increase protection efforts, such as removing standing water on their properties, dress in light-colored, long-sleeve clothing and closed-toed shoes and use insect repellent that contains DEET, Picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus. There has also been an uptick in West Nile Virus in Pinellas County sentinel chickens, the mosquito control reported. Officials will increase overnight truck treatments and daytime aerial treatments to combat the spread of viruses. Pinellas County has reported no human cases of West Nile virus this year. news.content_title: Stopping Dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses
news.content: ROANOKE, Va. ( WFXR ) - Dengue virus is a mosquito-borne illness that is normally found within tropical and sub-tropical areas. “Dengue viruses are spread to people through the bites of infected Aedes species mosquitoes,” says Dr. Julia Murphy, the State Public Health Veterinarian for the Virginia Department of Health. Mosquitos are considered vectors, meaning they’re organisms that can transmit diseases like dengue. “The one that spreads dengue the most efficiently and is considered the primary vector, if you will, of dengue virus is called Aedes Aegypti .” The species is native to Africa, but has appeared in the U.S. sporadically over the years as an invasive species. But, the U.S. is home to another species of Aedes mosquito; Aedes Albopictus. “The kind of Aedes mosquito that we have in abundance, is one that is a competent vector, you could say, but it's really not the main driver of dengue,” says Murphy. “It has a tendency to have a broader array of animals that it bites.” According to the World Health Organization, up to 400 million people around the world are at risk of becoming infected with dengue each year. Stopping the spread of vector-borne disease But unlike other viruses that spread from person to person, dengue spreads through mosquito bites. “You have a person who's infected with dengue, a person for whom dengue virus is circulating in their blood, a mosquito vector mosquito bites that person, “says Murphy. “Then after a relatively short period of time, that mosquito becomes infected with the dengue virus, and then if that mosquito bites another person, then that person gets infected.” Earlier this month, VDH confirmed the first case of dengue to be locally acquired here in Virginia. “We had a person in Northern Virginia who tested positive for the dengue virus and it appears that that infection was locally acquired, which means that person got infected in Virginia,” says Murphy. However, health officials say while this case is historic, it’s not unprecedented. “Over the years, 2010 through 2025, of all of the dengue virus infections that were reported as happening in people in the United States about 95% of them were travel associated,” says Murphy. VDH says while other potentially locally acquired cases are possible, it’s unlikely to see other cases at this time. Rabies: A closer look at the ‘deadliest disease’ “A lot of times that people at highest risk for additional transmission are folks in the household or folks who are in close proximity to a person with dengue virus in circulation,” says Murphy. Not everyone will have a reaction to the virus, as some people can appear asymptomatic to the infection. “Dengue can have a wide clinical spectrum that can occur,” says Murphy. “A lot of people don't become sick at all.” However, for those that are impacted by the disease, symptoms can vary. “Oftentimes they'll get a fever, that's a real hallmark of dengue,” says Murphy. “Then they have general aches and pains, sort of especially one feature of dengue can be in some people, a lot of pain behind the eyes, what's called retro ball pain.” Other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, muscle and joint pain, and a skin rash. “A smaller subset, probably around five-percent of people, can get what's called severe dengue,” says Murphy. “As the name would suggest, that is a severe illness that can result in things like shock and internal bleeding.” But while the risk of dengue spreading in the Commonwealth isn’t large, there are other mosquito-borne illnesses to be on the lookout for, including West Nile Virus. VDH says prevention is key, and there are plenty of tools people can use to not only help prevent dengue, but all mosquito-born illnesses. Back-to-school health, getting students ready for the school year “Some good prevention measures include things like when you're outdoors using mosquito repellent,” says Murphy. “What I would say is always follow the directions on the label.” Not every repellant is able to be used by all people, which is why experts say it’s important to know what ingredients are inside before spraying it on yourself, a child, or a pet. “It's important to look at that label and also look at the concentrations of of the various ingredients, because there are some precautions and recommendations for children,” says Murphy. “There may also be some cautions and recommendations associated with any pets you have.” Dr. Murphy suggests checking out the EPA’s website to determine which insect repellant is right for you. Another thing to utilize for protection is making sure you have screens on your windows, and that there aren’t any holes in them. “A lot of people like to have their door open or their windows open,” says Murphy. “Make sure that screen is in good repair, make sure your window screens are being repaired because you want to try to keep mosquitoes out.” Finally, it’s important to manage pools of water near your home, as stagnant water can become a breeding ground for mosquito larva. “You can help to drive down the populations of mosquitoes in and around your yard by helping to eliminate or routinely refreshing any standing water in your backyard,” says Murphy. Mosquito eggs need just seven to ten days to transition into a full-grown adult mosquito. “So if mosquitoes are laying their eggs in there and you're disrupting that cycle at least once a week, it'll really decrease the likelihood that any eggs that are in there would go on to become adults,” says Murphy. analysis.brief_en: This news report discusses the spread of dengue virus, a mosquito-borne illness primarily transmitted by Aedes Aegypti mosquitoes. It highlights that the first locally acquired case of dengue in Virginia was confirmed earlier this month, with the infection traced to Northern Virginia. Dr. Julia Murphy, the State Public Health Veterinarian for the Virginia Department of Health, explains that while dengue can have a wide clinical spectrum, most infections are travel-associated, with only about 5% of cases resulting in severe dengue, which can lead to shock and internal bleeding. Health officials emphasize that prevention is crucial, including the use of mosquito repellent, maintaining window screens, and eliminating stagnant water to reduce mosquito breeding. Although the risk of dengue spreading in the Commonwealth is not large, other mosquito-borne illnesses like West Nile virus are also a concern. The report underscores the importance of following guidelines to mitigate the spread of these diseases.

news.content_zh: 本新闻报道讨论了 登革病毒 的传播,这是一种主要由埃及伊蚊传播的蚊媒疾病。报告强调,本月早些时候确认了弗吉尼亚州首例本地感染登革热病例,感染源可追溯到弗吉尼亚州北部。弗吉尼亚州卫生部的州公共卫生兽医朱莉娅·墨菲 (Julia Murphy) 博士解释说,虽然登革热的临床范围很广,但大多数感染都与旅行有关,只有约 5% 的病例会导致 重症登革热,这可能会导致休克和内出血。卫生官员强调,预防至关重要,包括使用驱蚊剂、维护纱窗以及消除积水以减少蚊子繁殖。尽管登革热在英联邦传播的风险并不大,但西尼罗河病毒等其他蚊媒疾病也令人担忧。该报告强调了遵循指南以减轻这些疾病传播的重要性。

analysis.brief_en: The Hawaiʻi Department of Health reported another travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases in Hawaiʻi to seven in 2026. This case highlights the potential for dengue virus to spread through human travel, particularly in the wake of recent weather events like Hurricane Lala. The report does not specify the exact strain of the virus or provide details on the investigation or response measures taken. The case was identified as part of ongoing health monitoring efforts, and no explicit risk level was mentioned. The Department of Health continues to track and report on dengue cases, emphasizing the need for vigilance and preventive measures in the community.

news.content: The Brief Hillsborough County health officials have confirmed eight locally-acquired cases of dengue fever, up from two reported last week. Pinellas County has also confirmed two locally-acquired cases, prompting increased mosquito surveillance and treatment in the Palm Harbor area. Officials say residents can help by dumping standing water, using mosquito repellent and wearing loose-fitting, long-sleeved clothing. TAMPA, Fla. - Health officials are increasing mosquito control efforts across parts of the Tampa Bay area following a jump in locally acquired dengue fever cases. Tampa Bay dengue cases What we know The Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County announced an eighth confirmed locally-acquired case of dengue, while Pinellas County health officials have reported two locally-acquired cases. Both counties remain on alert as mosquito control teams increase surveillance and treatment. Locally-acquired cases mean the infections were transmitted by mosquitoes in the area rather than associated with travel. Undetected spread and testing Why it matters Dengue is spread through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquito. The Aedes aegypti mosquito is particularly concerning because it is active during the daytime, can breed in small amounts of standing water commonly found around homes, and thrives in neighborhoods. "It's a container breeder, which, unfortunately, means it likes to breed in things like buckets, planters, even trash you left out, maybe a kid's toy that gets left upside down," said Gabriela Henderson with Hillsborough County Mosquito Services. Henderson says even something as small as a bottle cap can become a breeding container for Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Adding to the challenge of combatting Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, Pinellas County officials say traditional adulticide treatments and aerial larviciding treatments are not effective in targeting these species. Neighborhood prevention steps What you can do Officials say one of the most effective steps residents can take is checking their property for standing water and dumping it out. That includes water collected in buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires, grill and pool covers, coolers and other containers. Even small amounts can provide a place for mosquitoes to breed. Residents should also: Wear light-colored, loose-fitting long sleeves and pants when possible. Use an EPA-registered mosquito repellent with an effective ingredient such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus. Repair damaged screens on windows and doors. Regularly dump or cover anything around the home that can collect rain or sprinkler water. "The biggest thing you can do is look for that standing water around your home," Henderson said. Recognizing dengue fever symptoms What are the symptoms of dengue? Dengue can cause a flu-like illness that includes fever, severe muscle and joint pain and, in some cases, a rash. Symptoms generally develop within about two weeks of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not spread directly from person to person through ordinary contact. Henderson said people who feel sick after recently being bitten by mosquitoes should tell their doctor. "If you're feeling under the weather, you notice you've been bit by mosquitoes recently, it's worth mentioning to your doctor because they can then give the proper test," Henderson said. "We work closely with the health department so they will be alerted, and then we are alerted as well." Pinellas County virus tracking What's being done Hillsborough County's health department and mosquito management teams say they are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts, including spraying, to reduce mosquito activity. In Pinellas County, mosquito control crews have increased inspections and treatments following the two confirmed cases. The county says crews are conducting daytime backpack fogging, daily surveillance and door-to-door inspections in affected areas. Pinellas County is also increasing mosquito control efforts because surveillance has detected an uptick in West Nile virus activity in sentinel chickens, which are used as an early warning system for mosquito-borne viruses. The county says no human cases of West Nile virus have been reported in Pinellas County so far this year. You can learn more about mosquito control efforts in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties via the following links. The Source Information in this article comes from the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County, Pinellas County Mosquito Control, the Florida Department of Health in Pinellas County, and prior reporting by FOX 13

news.content: Dengue or viral fever? Doctor explains why they may appear to be ‘similar’ and shares 9 signs to tell them apart Dengue fever should not be confused with viral fever, otherwise the health consequences may be adverse. Know how you can tell them apart. Published on: Aug 18, 2026, 10:32:24 IST By Adrija Dey Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link This monsoon season, you will hear almost everyone around you falling sick, with fever, sore throat, and vomiting. The most common response would be a lackadaisical one: that it is just a characteristic seasonal ailment. But this distinction is not for you to surmise otherwise; self-treatment can have adverse outcomes. ALSO READ: How to know if your medicine is genuine? 6 questions to ask before buying it Know the difference between viral fever and dengue fever. (Picture credit: Freepik) Dengue is also common during the monsoon season, and the symptoms can overlap with those of viral infection. Let's hear from a seasoned specialist with over 18 years of experience whose health advisory strictly cautions people from self-treating if they experience any flu-like symptoms. “Many people self-medicate and wait for symptoms to settle. Most viral fevers are self-limiting; dengue follows a very different course and can become life-threatening if warning signs are overlooked," Dr Chirag Tandon, director, internal medicine, ShardaCare-HealthCity, alerted, advocating for proactive initiative to get any symptoms evaluated by a health professional. Since dengue can be life-threatening if not treated on time can be dangerous. He ruled out self-medication at this time, even for viral infections, as many symptoms resemble. “The challenge is that both illnesses begin with similar symptoms, making it difficult to recognise when medical evaluation is necessary,” he instructed strictly. If you get it checked early, Dr Chirag informed that early diagnosis ensures successful treatment outcomes. Providing the key distinction, the doctor helped explain the root cause: “Dengue is due to the dengue virus, which is transmitted through the bite of an Aedes mosquito. On the other hand, viral fever refers to the condition characterized by fever due to different types of viruses.” Here are some of the questions related to dengue and viral fever that the doctor answered for us: Why do people confuse dengue and viral fever? Dr Chirag believed the most common symptom that causes confusion and leads many people to mistake dengue with viral fever is that both cause significant fever, aches in the body, and weakness. But dengue's signs are a bit higher on the severity scale than fever and can be recognised easily, despite the surface-level similarities. How to recognise if you may have dengue? To assess the symptoms, dengue's symptoms are more intense, while also being located in different regions. “Dengue symptoms include the sudden onset of high fever, severe headache, pain in the retro-orbital area, a high degree of muscle and joint pain, vomiting, and skin rash. When fever is caused by a viral infection, it usually features a sore throat, cough, rhinitis, and nasal blockage. However, respiratory symptoms in the case of dengue are relatively uncommon and constitute an important clinical clue,” Dr Chirag outlined the major differences that can help you understand if your symptoms lean more towards dengue or not. This necessary distinction also alleviates panic, as not all viral infections in the monsoon will be dengue. Further, the doctor provided the clinical picture of the laboratory findings. It is the last step to rule out dengue as a viral infection, and dengue appears very differently in blood tests. “Dengue often causes a reduction in platelet count and white blood cell count, but platelet numbers alone should never be used to judge disease severity. Equal importance is given to haematocrit levels, as a rising haematocrit may indicate plasma leakage, one of the hallmark complications of severe dengue. Viral fevers rarely produce this combination of laboratory findings.” Recurring fever should be taken as a sign to get tested for dengue. (Picture credit: Pexel) What is the most common misconception? As per the expert, dengue's recovery is often measured against fever, which is incorrect. He clarified and explained why it can be dangerous: “Many think dengue improves once fever subsides, but the timeframe between the third and the seventh day of the disease, when temperatures begin to stabilize, is often the most serious. At the time, plasma leakage could occur, resulting in an increased possibility of shock, internal bleeding, and organ malfunction.” This clinical insight is crucial as it tells us that even a seemingly recovering patient can deteriorate rapidly. Other than fever, which other symptoms indicate dengue? Dizziness is one of the symptoms of dengue. (Picture credit: Shutterstock) Dengue fever is accompanied by several other ‘warning signs,' which the doctor advised never to ignore. He cautioned about these signs, which may progressively get worse and require hospital-based management: Persistent vomiting Severe abdominal pain Increasing drowsiness Unusual restlessness Bleeding from the gums or nose Reduced urine output Cold clammy skin Breathlessness Sudden dizziness How are the treatments of dengue and viral fevers different? Just to put into perspective, so you know how far apart the treatments are, the doctor pointed out that dengue fever needs a combination of careful administration of fluids and continuous monitoring of the condition, and patients are asked to stay away from medications like ibuprofen and aspirin since they can increase the risk of bleeding. But regular viral fevers go down with the expert-recommended paracetamol dosage. Note to readers: This article is for informational purposes only and not a substitute for professional medical advice. NewsPricingLoginSign up News·Business Business GSK secures preclinical dengue antibody from Chugai Edited by Robert McTiernan·August 19, 2026·2 min read GSK has secured an exclusive, worldwide license from Japan-based Chugai Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (Tokyo: 4519) for AID351, a preclinical pan-serotype anti-dengue virus monoclonal antibody, converting an exploratory collaboration signed in January 2025 into a full development commitment. Under the agreement, GSK assumes responsibility for Phase I and subsequent clinical trials and manufacturing, while Chugai retains eligibility for royalties on future product sales and a share of any sublicensing income GSK collects from third parties. No upfront payment or total deal value was disclosed. AID351 was originated through a joint project between Chugai Pharmabody Research (CPR), the company's Singapore-based discovery subsidiary, and ASTAR Singapore Immunology Network (ASTAR SIgN), with the National University of Singapore contributing the lead antibody. Chugai applied its proprietary antibody engineering technologies to optimize the molecule, which the company describes as designed to neutralize all four dengue serotypes. The project received grant funding twice from the Global Health Innovative Technology (GHIT) Fund. No approved monoclonal antibody treatment for dengue fever currently exists; the approved products in the space — Sanofi's Dengvaxia and Takeda's Qdenga — are vaccines rather than therapeutics. The non-disclosure of deal financials, combined with the fact that the counterparty is GSK's Global Health unit rather than its commercial pharma division, is consistent with the access-oriented economics that typically govern neglected tropical disease partnerships — where royalty rates are often tiered for lower-income markets and upfront payments may be nominal or replaced by development cost commitments. GSK's interest in dengue predates the AID351 collaboration. The company has pursued dengue vaccines since at least the early 2000s and in 2009 established a vaccine R&D collaboration with Brazil's Fiocruz, while a separate program with the US Army advanced a purified inactivated dengue vaccine into Phase I trials in 2012. AID351 shifts that longstanding interest from prevention toward treatment and sits within GSK's broader Global Health strategy, under which the company committed GBP 1 billion over 10 years from 2022 to accelerate R&D targeting diseases including malaria, tuberculosis, antimicrobial resistance, and neglected tropical diseases. NewsPricingLoginSign up News·Business Business GSK secures preclinical dengue antibody from Chugai Edited by Robert McTiernan·August 19, 2026·2 min read GSK has secured an exclusive, worldwide license from Japan-based Chugai Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (Tokyo: 4519) for AID351, a preclinical pan-serotype anti-dengue virus monoclonal antibody, converting an exploratory collaboration signed in January 2025 into a full development commitment. Under the agreement, GSK assumes responsibility for Phase I and subsequent clinical trials and manufacturing, while Chugai retains eligibility for royalties on future product sales and a share of any sublicensing income GSK collects from third parties. No upfront payment or total deal value was disclosed. AID351 was originated through a joint project between Chugai Pharmabody Research (CPR), the company's Singapore-based discovery subsidiary, and ASTAR Singapore Immunology Network (ASTAR SIgN), with the National University of Singapore contributing the lead antibody. Chugai applied its proprietary antibody engineering technologies to optimize the molecule, which the company describes as designed to neutralize all four dengue serotypes. The project received grant funding twice from the Global Health Innovative Technology (GHIT) Fund. No approved monoclonal antibody treatment for dengue fever currently exists; the approved products in the space — Sanofi's Dengvaxia and Takeda's Qdenga — are vaccines rather than therapeutics. The non-disclosure of deal financials, combined with the fact that the counterparty is GSK's Global Health unit rather than its commercial pharma division, is consistent with the access-oriented economics that typically govern neglected tropical disease partnerships — where royalty rates are often tiered for lower-income markets and upfront payments may be nominal or replaced by development cost commitments. GSK's interest in dengue predates the AID351 collaboration. The company has pursued dengue vaccines since at least the early 2000s and in 2009 established a vaccine R&D collaboration with Brazil's Fiocruz, while a separate program with the US Army advanced a purified inactivated dengue vaccine into Phase I trials in 2012. AID351 shifts that longstanding interest from prevention toward treatment and sits within GSK's broader Global Health strategy, under which the company committed GBP 1 billion over 10 years from 2022 to accelerate R&D targeting diseases including malaria, tuberculosis, antimicrobial resistance, and neglected tropical diseases. news.content: Quảng cáo của DTads Thursday, 20 August 2026 Tiếng Việt RSS VIETNAM TODAY Business Society Education Environment LIFESTYLE Travel Entertainment Food & Drink CULTURE AND SPORT Culture Sport COMMUNITY MULTI MEDIA Copied VIETNAM TODAY HCM City sees rise in dengue cases, severe infections August 17, 2026 - 03:47 PM HCM City has recorded more than 25,700 dengue cases this year, with infections remaining high and doctors warning that patients can deteriorate rapidly even after their fever subsides. The city reported 1,097 cases in the past week, up 7 per cent from the average of the previous four weeks, bringing the total to 25,774 through week 32. Children's Hospital No. 2 recorded 270 dengue outpatients and 104 discharged inpatients from August 1-13, with 25 children still receiving treatment on August 14. According to Vu Thi Thuy Duong, deputy head of the department, dengue cases among children were rising, including some severe cases. Xuyen A General Hospital receives around 15-20 dengue patients a day, with about one-third requiring admission. Meanwhile, the HCM City Hospital for Tropical Diseases, around 120 dengue patients were being treated on August 14, with severe cases receiving intensive care. Van Thi Xuan Quynh, deputy head of the department, said some patients had developed dengue shock, organ damage and severe gastrointestinal bleeding, with some requiring transfer to higher-level hospitals. There is no specific treatment for dengue, with care focused on supportive treatment and managing complications. Doctors said early detection and close monitoring were therefore critical. Nguyen Thanh Phong, deputy director of the hospital, said dengue could become severe as fever subsides. Plasma leakage can reduce circulating blood volume, causing low blood pressure and shock. Prolonged shock can lead to multiple organ damage, blood-clotting disorders and bleeding, significantly increasing the risk of death. Severe patients may require intensive care, respiratory support, dialysis, blood transfusions or blood products, depending on their condition. Phong noted that the disappearance of fever did not mean a patient had recovered. People with obesity or underlying medical conditions may also face a higher risk of complications and more difficult treatment. Doctors advised people with fever to seek medical attention, while dengue patients should attend follow-up appointments, particularly during the critical phase even after fever subsides. They also recommended dengue vaccination, particularly for eligible people at higher risk, in accordance with medical guidance. During the rainy season, residents are advised to eliminate mosquito breeding sites by covering or removing containers that collect water, regularly cleaning water storage containers and eliminating mosquito larvae. The HCM City Centre for Disease Control also recommends using mosquito nets, including during the day, wearing long-sleeved clothing and taking other appropriate measures to prevent mosquito bites. Residents should cooperate with mosquito-control and spraying campaigns organised by local health authorities to help reduce dengue transmission. analysis.time: HCM City has recorded more than 25,700 dengue cases this year, with infections remaining high and doctors warning that patients can deteriorate rapidly even after their fever subsides. The city reported 1,097 cases in the past week, up 7 per cent from the average of the previous four weeks, bringing the total to 25,774 through week 32. On August 14, 25 children were still receiving treatment at Children's Hospital No. 2, and around 120 dengue patients were being treated at the HCM City Hospital for Tropical Diseases.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is occurring in Ho Chi Minh City (HCM City), Vietnam. Dengue cases are reported among children and adults, with specific mention of Children's Hospital No. 2 and the HCM City Hospital for Tropical Diseases. The affected population includes residents of HCM City, particularly those in areas with high mosquito activity.
analysis.event: HCM City has experienced a significant rise in dengue cases, with severe infections reported. Doctors have warned that patients can deteriorate rapidly even after their fever subsides, and some have developed dengue shock, organ damage, and severe gastrointestinal bleeding. The city's health authorities are monitoring the situation closely.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of week 32, HCM City has recorded 25,774 dengue cases, with 1,097 reported in the past week. Children's Hospital No. 2 had 270 dengue outpatients and 104 discharged inpatients from August 1-13, with 25 children still in treatment on August 14. Severe cases require intensive care, respiratory support, dialysis, blood transfusions, or other interventions. The risk of complications is higher for individuals with obesity or underlying medical conditions.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health authorities in HCM City are advising residents to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, use mosquito nets, and wear long-sleeved clothing to prevent bites. They are also recommending dengue vaccination for eligible individuals. Doctors are urging early detection and close monitoring of patients, especially during the critical phase even after fever subsides. The situation remains under active investigation and management.

analysis.brief_en: HCM City is experiencing a surge in dengue cases, with over 25,700 reported this year and 1,097 in the past week, marking a 7% increase from the previous four weeks. The outbreak has led to severe infections, including dengue shock, organ damage, and gastrointestinal bleeding, with some patients requiring transfer to higher-level hospitals. Children's Hospital No. 2 and the HCM City Hospital for Tropical Diseases are treating a significant number of patients, with 25 children still receiving care on August 14. Doctors emphasize that fever subsiding does not mean recovery, and early detection is critical. Health authorities recommend eliminating mosquito breeding sites, using mosquito nets, and vaccination for high-risk groups. The situation remains under active monitoring and management, with no specific treatment available, only supportive care for complications.

supplementary_news.content_title: Stopping Dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses
supplementary_news.content: WFXRtv Stopping Dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses Nicholas Noleff 3 days ago ROANOKE, Va. (WFXR) – Dengue virus is a mosquito-borne illness that is normally found within tropical and sub-tropical areas. “Dengue viruses are spread to people through the bites of infected Aedes species mosquitoes,” says Dr. Julia Murphy, the State Public Health Veterinarian for the Virginia Department of Health. Mosquitos are considered vectors, meaning they’re organisms that can transmit diseases like dengue. “The one that spreads dengue the most efficiently and is considered the primary vector, if you will, of dengue virus is called Aedes Aegypti.” The species is native to Africa, but has appeared in the U.S. sporadically over the years as an invasive species. But, the U.S. is home to another species of Aedes mosquito; Aedes Albopictus. “The kind of Aedes mosquito that we have in abundance, is one that is a competent vector, you could say, but it’s really not the main driver of dengue,” says Murphy. “It has a tendency to have a broader array of animals that it bites.” According to the World Health Organization, up to 400 million people around the world are at risk of becoming infected with dengue each year. But unlike other viruses that spread from person to person, dengue spreads through mosquito bites. “You have a person who’s infected with dengue, a person for whom dengue virus is circulating in their blood, a mosquito vector mosquito bites that person, “says Murphy. “Then after a relatively short period of time, that mosquito becomes infected with the dengue virus, and then if that mosquito bites another person, then that person gets infected.” Earlier this month, VDH confirmed the first case of dengue to be locally acquired here in Virginia. “We had a person in Northern Virginia who tested positive for the dengue virus and it appears that that infection was locally acquired, which means that person got infected in Virginia,” says Murphy. However, health officials say while this case is historic, it’s not unprecedented. “Over the years, 2010 through 2025, of all of the dengue virus infections that were reported as happening in people in the United States about 95% of them were travel associated,” says Murphy. VDH says while other potentially locally acquired cases are possible, it’s unlikely to see other cases at this time. “A lot of times that people at highest risk for additional transmission are folks in the household or folks who are in close proximity to a person with dengue virus in circulation,” says Murphy. Not everyone will have a reaction to the virus, as some people can appear asymptomatic to the infection. “Dengue can have a wide clinical spectrum that can occur,” says Murphy. “A lot of people don’t become sick at all.” However, for those that are impacted by the disease, symptoms can vary. “Oftentimes they’ll get a fever, that’s a real hallmark of dengue,” says Murphy. “Then they have general aches and pains, sort of especially one feature of dengue can be in some people, a lot of pain behind the eyes, what’s called retro ball pain.” Other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, muscle and joint pain, and a skin rash. “A smaller subset, probably around five-percent of people, can get what’s called severe dengue,” says Murphy. “As the name would suggest, that is a severe illness that can result in things like shock and internal bleeding.” But while the risk of dengue spreading in the Commonwealth isn’t large, there are other mosquito-borne illnesses to be on the lookout for, including West Nile Virus. VDH says prevention is key, and there are plenty of tools people can use to not only help prevent dengue, but all mosquito-born illnesses. “Some good prevention measures include things like when you’re outdoors using mosquito repellent,” says Murphy. “What I would say is always follow the directions on the label.” Not every repellant is able to be used by all people, which is why experts say it’s important to know what ingredients are inside before spraying it on yourself, a child, or a pet. “It’s important to look at that label and also look at the concentrations of of the various ingredients, because there are some precautions and recommendations for children,” says Murphy. “There may also be some cautions and recommendations associated with any pets you have.” Dr. Murphy suggests checking out the EPA’s website to determine which insect repellant is right for you. Another thing to utilize for protection is making sure you have screens on your windows, and that there aren’t any holes in them. “A lot of people like to have their door open or their windows open,” says Murphy. “Make sure that screen is in good repair, make sure your window screens are being repaired because you want to try to keep mosquitoes out.” Finally, it’s important to manage pools of water near your home, as stagnant water can become a breeding ground for mosquito larva. “You can help to drive down the populations of mosquitoes in and around your yard by helping to eliminate or routinely refreshing any standing water in your backyard,” says Murphy. Mosquito eggs need just seven to ten days to transition into a full-grown adult mosquito. “So if mosquitoes are laying their eggs in there and you’re disrupting that cycle at least once a week, it’ll really decrease the likelihood that any eggs that are in there would go on to become adults,” says Murphy. PC: by Wendy Osher The Hawaiʻi Department of Health has identified a new travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases reported in Hawaiʻi to seven in 2026. The individual was exposed to the virus while traveling internationally in a region where dengue is common. No connection to any prior cases in Hawaiʻi has been identified. DOH teams have been deployed to conduct inspections and implement mosquito-control measures in the affected area. Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low. However, with recent flooding from Tropical Cyclone Lala and anticipated rain in the forecast, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases. More information about mosquito control is available on the vector control website. Dengue virus is transmitted from an infected person to a mosquito and then to another person. While Hawaiʻi is home to mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the disease is not endemic, or established, in the state; cases are currently limited to travelers. Of the seven dengue cases reported in Hawaiʻi in 2026, all have involved travel to Pacific island countries and territories. Dengue is a year-round risk in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, including Brazil and Mexico; Asia, including the Philippines; the Middle East; Africa; and several Pacific islands, including American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations in the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are also affected. Some countries are reporting higher-than-usual numbers of dengue cases, including Bolivia, Colombia, Samoa, Tonga, New Caledonia, Cambodia, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Kenya. Travelers should review up-to-date, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. For current travel health information and guidance, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s travel website. Anyone planning to travel to or who has recently visited an area with dengue risk may be at risk for infection. The CDC advises travelers to take standard precautions when visiting such areas. These include using an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long pants outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms, rooms with window screens or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas with dengue risk should take precautions to prevent mosquito bites for three weeks. If dengue symptoms develop within two weeks of returning, travelers should seek medical evaluation. Symptoms of dengue can range from mild to severe and include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches. Symptoms typically last two to seven days. While severe illness can occur, most people recover within a week. Individuals who have recently traveled and are experiencing these symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection are advised to call the Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. In areas with suspected or confirmed dengue cases, DOH personnel from the Vector Control Branch conduct inspections and mosquito-reduction activities. Reducing mosquito populations lowers the risk of dengue transmission to others. In areas without reported dengue cases, eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home is an important preventive measure. Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water to breed. Common breeding sites include buckets, water-catching plants such as bromeliads, small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside. Prevent standing water from collecting around homes and workplaces by emptying containers and other items where mosquitoes can lay eggs. supplementary_news.content: newsinfo / Headlines Headlines Baguio eyes mosquito bacteria to curb dengue Technology using Wolbachia to inhibit virus from multiplying inside Aedes aegypti mosquito shows promising results in other countries By: Vincent Cabreza - Reporter / @Inquirer_Baguio Philippine Daily Inquirer / 04:35 AM August 19, 2026 TAKING ACTION City health workers conduct dengue prevention activities in Tacloban as cases rise. In Baguio, where dengue cases are also increasing, health officials are exploring Wolbachia technology as another tool to prevent mosquitoes from transmitting the virus. —Tacloban City Health Office BAGUIO CITY, Philippines —The city is being considered a pilot site for a technology that uses the naturally occurring Wolbachia bacteria to prevent mosquitoes from transmitting dengue, as cities including Tacloban intensify efforts to contain rising infections. The city council was told Monday that two companies that invested in applications of this research have expressed interest in using the city as a model site for the technology before potentially expanding it to other parts of the country. Baguio chief epidemiologist Dr. Donabel Tubera Panes said the city government participated in the Philippine Wolbachia Dialogue on June 23, where disease experts and representatives of companies discussed the bacteria’s potential in dengue control. Article continues after this advertisement Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterium found naturally in many insects, can inhibit the dengue virus from multiplying inside the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary vector of dengue. FEATURED STORIES NEWSINFO Walang Pasok: Class suspensions Aug. 19 (Wednesday) due to bad weather NEWSINFO Alleged Zamboanga City school shooter dead -- DILG NEWSINFO BOC relieves Zamboanga school shooter’s father from Customs post READ: DOH logs over 7,400 dengue cases in January, down 71% from last year “What laboratories in Australia and California (in America) did was to inject the bacteria into an Aedes mosquito, and subsequently new generations of mosquitoes would no longer be infected and would not transmit dengue,” Panes told the council. She said the technology has shown promising results in countries that have adopted it. In Australia, where Wolbachia has been introduced into mosquito populations for about 15 years, dengue cases declined by 77 percent and hospitalizations by 86 percent, Panes said. The bacteria is not genetically modified and does not harm humans, she said. Article continues after this advertisement Baguio has recorded 543 dengue cases since January. Data dating back to 2005 show that infections in the city tend to spike every two to three years, with health officials expecting this year’s cases to peak around mid-August before tapering off by mid-October. “Dengue is here to stay,” Panes said, adding that the experience of countries, such as Indonesia, Singapore and Australia, suggests that Wolbachia could be “the missing link in our dengue management.” Article continues after this advertisement Surveillance In Tacloban City, health authorities have intensified dengue surveillance and prevention after cases reached 272 as of Aug. 8, up 31 percent from the 208 cases recorded during the same period last year. City Health Officer Dr. Jaime Opinion Jr. said the increase prompted the city to place its public health response under a code blue alert, allowing health authorities to strengthen disease surveillance, prevention measures and preparedness. “While the increase in dengue cases in the city is alarming compared with the same period last year, it is not alarming to the point of an emergency because we have not recorded any deaths,” Opinion said. He attributed the rise partly to Tacloban’s pattern of experiencing higher dengue cases every three years, as well as inadequate water supply and changing weather conditions. “We are feeling the effects of El Niño, with periods of heavy rain followed by extreme heat. The lack of water supply also contributes because residents tend to store rainwater in containers, which can become breeding places for mosquitoes that transmit dengue,” Opinion said. With assistance from the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office, the City Health Office has been conducting fogging operations in barangays where dengue clustering has been reported or where at least two cases have been recorded. Health personnel are also conducting antidengue spraying in homes, particularly in dark and poorly ventilated areas where mosquitoes may hide. Opinion said hospitals in Tacloban had also admitted 374 dengue patients from outside the city, indicating that local health facilities are serving patients from neighboring provinces. Community effort Across the Cordillera region, the Department of Health recorded 4,436 dengue cases from Jan. 4 to Aug. 8. Cases increased by 9 percent in Abra, 23 percent in Benguet, 34 percent in Kalinga and 44 percent in Ifugao. Dengue is transmitted mainly through bites from infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which commonly breed in stagnant water found in discarded containers, tires, cans and uncovered water storage vessels. Opinion urged residents to regularly inspect and clean their homes and surroundings and eliminate areas where water can accumulate. Residents were also advised to wear long-sleeved clothing, use mosquito repellents and install screens or mosquito nets where possible. Early consultation is encouraged when symptoms develop. It is not the responsibility of the city government or health authorities alone,” Opinion said. —WITH A REPORT FROM JOEY A. supplementary_news.content: by PERPETUA ETYANG Friday August 7, 2026 Image generated with AI The United States has issued a travel health alert for Kenya following a rise in dengue fever cases, urging travellers to take extra precautions against mosquito bites. In a health alert issued by the US Embassy in Nairobi, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) listed Kenya among countries reporting a higher number of dengue cases in its updated Travel Health Notice. The advisory identifies Kenya's coastal region, as well as Wajir and Garissa counties, as areas where travellers should exercise caution. "Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in tropical and subtropical climates that can lead to fever, aches and pains, nausea, and rashes," the embassy said. The embassy urged travellers to consult the CDC's travel health advisories before travelling to affected areas and to take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Recommended precautions include using an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long trousers when outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms or rooms fitted with window screens. The alert comes as health authorities continue to monitor dengue infections in several parts of the country, with the disease primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The US Embassy advised travellers seeking more information to consult the CDC's travel health guidance or contact the agency directly before visiting affected areas. Dengue is a viral infection that affects millions of people worldwide and is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Once diagnosed, it is important to follow medical advice closely, monitor symptoms, and prioritise rest. Adequate hydration plays a crucial role in preventing complications, while nutritious meals help support the body's recovery process. Patients should remain alert to warning signs that may indicate worsening illness and seek immediate medical assistance when necessary. In some cases, hospitalisation may be recommended to ensure close monitoring and appropriate treatment during the recovery period. In May, Garissa county embarked on a massive fumigation exercise aimed at containing the spread of dengue fever following a recent outbreak that has seen several residents hospitalised at the Garissa County Referral Hospital. The two-week exercise, which officially kicked off on Thursday, will involve public health officials fumigating drainage areas, public institutions, schools, markets and other public spaces across Garissa township in an effort to eliminate mosquitoes responsible for spreading the disease. Health officials said samples taken from patients admitted at the Garissa County Referral Hospital confirmed infections of dengue fever, a viral disease transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which commonly breeds in stagnant water. Speaking to the press after overseeing the launch of the fumigation exercise, Hassan Abdullahi, who was representing the Medical Officer of Health said laboratory tests conducted at the National Public Health Laboratory confirmed the outbreak after 28 out of 40 samples collected from both public and private health facilities tested positive for dengue fever

supplementary_news.content: Travel Sports Entertainment Environment Politics Education Community Health Crime Business Traffic Real Estate Search Wednesday, August 19, 2026 About Us Contact Us Advertising information Liquor Licenses Classifieds Archives Facebook Instagram Linkedin Pinterest Twitter Youtube Travel Sports Entertainment Environment Politics Education Community Health Crime Business Traffic Real Estate Search GovernmentHealth MoHW Advises Public on Dengue Prevention During Rainy Season Monday, August 17th, 2026 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Press Release, Belmopan, August 17, 2026. The Ministry of Health and Wellness reminds the public that the rainy season increases the risk of dengue transmission. Dengue is spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in stagnant water commonly found in containers around homes and communities. Dengue can cause mild to severe illness and, in some cases, can be fatal. Common symptoms of dengue include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, skin rash, and, in severe cases, bleeding or difficulty breathing. The Ministry urges residents to seek medical attention immediately if you are experiencing symptoms. Dengue prevention is a shared responsibility. Checking homes, yards, workplaces, and communities for mosquito breeding sites can significantly reduce the risk of dengue transmission. Residents should take the following preventive measures: • Empty, cover, or remove containers that collect water around homes and businesses. • Remove discarded containers, tires, bottles, cans, and other items that can collect rainwater. • Keep drains, yards, vacant lots, and surroundings free of excessive vegetation, garbage, and debris. • Use mosquito repellents as directed. • Wear long-sleeved clothing, particularly during the early morning and late afternoon when mosquitoes are most active. • Ensure doors and windows are properly screened to prevent mosquito entry. The Ministry of Health and Wellness continues to work closely with communities, local authorities, and partners to strengthen surveillance and vector control activities throughout the country. Subscribe Health News Florida Mosquito control ramps up as dengue fever cases rise in Hillsborough and Pinellas WUSF | By Nancy Guan Published August 14, 2026 at 4:50 AM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 1:02 Nancy Guan / WUSF Mosquitoes caught in special traps are taken to a lab, where they're frozen and killed. The females, which transmit disease, are separated and sent to a lab that tests for dengue. Eight people in Hillsborough and two in Pinellas recently contracted the mosquito-borne illness locally, officials say. Both counties are under alerts. The disease is not endemic to the Tampa Bay region. The Tampa Bay region is experiencing more locally acquired cases of dengue fever than usual this year. The Florida Department of Health reported eight cases in Hillsborough County and two in Pinellas County so far, and both are on a mosquito-borne illness alert. For Pinellas, it's the first case of locally acquired dengue in over 15 years, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Pinellas doesn't have any modern history of having dengue in the county," said Alyssa Berro, the county's mosquito control manager. "So this is one of those cases [where] somebody has returned from somewhere they got bit. And then got bit by our mosquitoes, which then started the transmission in this area." Symptoms of dengue typically appear 15 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. The illness, also referred to as bone-break fever, can come with joint and muscle pain. Other symptoms include pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting and rash. Local versus travel-associated Dengue is not what experts call endemic – or regularly found – in Florida. Typically, people will contract dengue while traveling to other countries, rather than getting bit by an infected mosquito in the Tampa Bay area. Dengue is not contagious between humans, but it can spread if a mosquito bites someone with the illness and becomes a carrier. ALSO READ: Locally acquired cases of mosquito-borne dengue reported in Palm Beach, Miami-Dade The insect can then spread the disease by biting others or breeding more dengue-carrying mosquitos. Between 2010 to 2025, Hillsborough County reported 277 dengue cases due to travel and nine locally acquired cases. The eight locally acquired cases this year were reported within the last two weeks. "And that's what makes this such a big change, is that it is going around in the mosquitoes in our county," said Gabriela Henderson, community relations coordinator for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management. WUSF file A female Aedes aegypti mosquito, the primary spreader of dengue fever, feeds on a human. Mosquito treatment Efforts to control the spread are underway. Mosquito control for both counties are treating areas by truck and helicopter aerial sprays. Pinellas and Hillsborough residents can check which neighborhoods have been treated online. ALSO READ: Before you swat that mosquito this summer, take a picture of it Technicians are also visiting homes and businesses to treat mosquito-prone areas by hand. County health officials are encouraging residents to remove any standing water around their homes. "They like to lay their eggs near humans in things like buckets, toys we might leave outside in the rain, tarps, planters," said Henderson. "Anything that can hold even just a bottle cap-sized amount of water is enough for mosquitoes to go through their whole life cycle." Henderson said tires are a common breeding ground for mosquitos since they tend to hold water. Nancy Guan / WUSF The BG trap is one type of mosquito trap being used to catch adult mosquitoes. The mosquito control teams also manage a number of mosquito traps across each county. These BG traps – or biogent traps – have components that mimic human scent and emit carbon dioxide to lure in adult mosquitos. The trapped mosquitos are then taken back to the lab, where they're frozen and killed. The female mosquitoes, which are the only mosquitoes that bite humans and animals, are separated and sent to a lab that tests for dengue. Henderson said one mosquito from Hillsborough has come back positive. Protect yourself The breed of mosquitoes carrying dengue is the Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. These dengue-carrying mosquitoes will bite during the daytime, not just in the evening, and tend to stay low to the ground. That makes them harder to avoid and detect. Berro said homeowners should check their yards once a week for standing water. She recommended people wear light-colored clothing that covers the legs and arms when they go outside, and to use insect repellent approved by the Environment Protection Agency that contains DEET, IR3535, picaridin or oil of lemon eucalyptus. "We call those the three D's: to dump, dress and defend," said Berro.
