supplementary_news.content: ROANOKE, Va. ( WFXR ) - Dengue virus is a mosquito-borne illness that is normally found within tropical and sub-tropical areas. “Dengue viruses are spread to people through the bites of infected Aedes species mosquitoes,” says Dr. Julia Murphy, the State Public Health Veterinarian for the Virginia Department of Health. Mosquitos are considered vectors, meaning they’re organisms that can transmit diseases like dengue. “The one that spreads dengue the most efficiently and is considered the primary vector, if you will, of dengue virus is called Aedes Aegypti .” The species is native to Africa, but has appeared in the U.S. sporadically over the years as an invasive species. But, the U.S. is home to another species of Aedes mosquito; Aedes Albopictus. “The kind of Aedes mosquito that we have in abundance, is one that is a competent vector, you could say, but it's really not the main driver of dengue,” says Murphy. “It has a tendency to have a broader array of animals that it bites.” According to the World Health Organization, up to 400 million people around the world are at risk of becoming infected with dengue each year. Stopping the spread of vector-borne disease But unlike other viruses that spread from person to person, dengue spreads through mosquito bites. “You have a person who's infected with dengue, a person for whom dengue virus is circulating in their blood, a mosquito vector mosquito bites that person, “says Murphy. “Then after a relatively short period of time, that mosquito becomes infected with the dengue virus, and then if that mosquito bites another person, then that person gets infected.” Earlier this month, VDH confirmed the first case of dengue to be locally acquired here in Virginia. “We had a person in Northern Virginia who tested positive for the dengue virus and it appears that that infection was locally acquired, which means that person got infected in Virginia,” says Murphy. However, health officials say while this case is historic, it’s not unprecedented. “Over the years, 2010 through 2025, of all of the dengue virus infections that were reported as happening in people in the United States about 95% of them were travel associated,” says Murphy. VDH says while other potentially locally acquired cases are possible, it’s unlikely to see other cases at this time. Rabies: A closer look at the ‘deadliest disease’ “A lot of times that people at highest risk for additional transmission are folks in the household or folks who are in close proximity to a person with dengue virus in circulation,” says Murphy. Not everyone will have a reaction to the virus, as some people can appear asymptomatic to the infection. “Dengue can have a wide clinical spectrum that can occur,” says Murphy. “A lot of people don't become sick at all.” However, for those that are impacted by the disease, symptoms can vary. “Oftentimes they'll get a fever, that's a real hallmark of dengue,” says Murphy. “Then they have general aches and pains, sort of especially one feature of dengue can be in some people, a lot of pain behind the eyes, what's called retro ball pain.” Other symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, muscle and joint pain, and a skin rash. “A smaller subset, probably around five-percent of people, can get what's called severe dengue,” says Murphy. “As the name would suggest, that is a severe illness that can result in things like shock and internal bleeding.” But while the risk of dengue spreading in the Commonwealth isn’t large, there are other mosquito-borne illnesses to be on the lookout for, including West Nile Virus. VDH says prevention is key, and there are plenty of tools people can use to not only help prevent dengue, but all mosquito-born illnesses. Back-to-school health, getting students ready for the school year “Some good prevention measures include things like when you're outdoors using mosquito repellent,” says Murphy. “What I would say is always follow the directions on the label.” Not every repellant is able to be used by all people, which is why experts say it’s important to know what ingredients are inside before spraying it on yourself, a child, or a pet. “It's important to look at that label and also look at the concentrations of of the various ingredients, because there are some precautions and recommendations for children,” says Murphy. “There may also be some cautions and recommendations associated with any pets you have.” Dr. Murphy suggests checking out the EPA’s website to determine which insect repellant is right for you. Another thing to utilize for protection is making sure you have screens on your windows, and that there aren’t any holes in them. “A lot of people like to have their door open or their windows open,” says Murphy. “Make sure that screen is in good repair, make sure your window screens are being repaired because you want to try to keep mosquitoes out.” Finally, it’s important to manage pools of water near your home, as stagnant water can become a breeding ground for mosquito larva. “You can help to drive down the populations of mosquitoes in and around your yard by helping to eliminate or routinely refreshing any standing water in your backyard,” says Murphy. Mosquito eggs need just seven to ten days to transition into a full-grown adult mosquito. “So if mosquitoes are laying their eggs in there and you're disrupting that cycle at least once a week, it'll really decrease the likelihood that any eggs that are in there would go on to become adults,” says Murphy. amid rains Steffy Thevar / Aug 19, 2026, 00:36 IST Comments Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large Pune: Civic and private hospitals have reported an increase in vector-borne infections due to stagnant water and high humidity fuelling mosquito breeding across the city amid rains.Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) officials said they had intensified anti-larval drives and fogging at identified hotspots to curb a further spread, even as doctors advised immediate medical attention for high fever, rashes or severe pain. Authorities have urged residents to clear puddles, cover stored water, use mosquito nets and repellents, stay hydrated and seek early testing.PMC assistant health officer Dr Rajesh Dighe said, ”In the first half of Aug, 234 suspected dengue cases and 13 laboratory confirmed cases were reported. In July, there were a total of 323 suspected cases and 12 confirmed ones. We have also seen a jump in chikungunya cases. Seven cases were reported within the first fortnight of Aug, compared to one in July. We have been issuing notices to commercial and residential establishments with evident lacunae in measures to prevent mosquito breeding.”Private hospitals have also seen a surge in the number of patients coming in with fever, body ache, weakness and other flu-like symptoms over the last few weeks. Consultant of internal medicine at Jupiter Hospital Dr Vineet Rao said, “Dengue and chikungunya remain important concerns during monsoon, alongside malaria and other infections that can cause similar symptoms. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Retirees Are Ditching $600 Prescriptions for These $39 German-Engineered GlassesTrending Learn More Undo It is important to be alert and not brush off a persistent or high fever as just a viral. It is particularly essential in case of children, elderly people and pregnant women or those with diabetes and other underlying conditions as they are more vulnerable to complications and may need closer monitoring.”Consultant in paediatrics and neonatology at Surya Mother & Child Super Specialty Hospital Dr Jayant Khandare said, “We have seen many cases of dengue recently. It can worsen as the fever begins to settle. Persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, bleeding, unusual drowsiness or restlessness require urgent medical review. Chikungunya often causes severe joint pain that may continue after the fever. We monitor infants, pregnant women and patients with underlying illnesses especially closely. Since the infections can appear similar initially, suspected chikungunya should be managed as dengue until dengue is excluded. Aspirin and ibuprofen should be avoided.”Patients with high-grade or persistent fever, significant dehydration, severe body or joint pain or symptoms that are worsening should consult a doctor at the earliest, advised experts.Dr Amit Tungenwar, consultant physician at Noble Hospitals and Research Centre, said, “It is important to understand that a low platelet count alone does not determine severity of dengue. Patients should not panic or self-medicate. The overall clinical condition, hydration status and presence of warning signs are important to determine the need for hospitalisation. Prevention remains important during monsoon. People should remove stagnant water from around their homes and workplaces, use protective clothing and keep water-storage containers properly covered. Early medical consultation, appropriate monitoring and preventive measures can go a long way to reduce complications from these infections.” You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in Pune Stay updated with the latest Pune news. supplementary_news.content_title: Army receives 2,900 dengue vaccine doses for troops
supplementary_news.content: The Royal Thai Army Medical Department has received 2,900 dengue vaccine doses for personnel serving in areas at high risk of outbreaks and those considered at risk of developing severe dengue. The vaccines were donated by the Medical Association of Thailand under Royal Patronage at a ceremony at the Army Medical Department Headquarters on August 5, 2026. Prof Dr Keerati Chareancholvanich, president of the Medical Association of Thailand, led the association’s delegation, while Lt Gen Kriengchai Prasongsukarn, chief of the Royal Thai Army Medical Department, presided over the ceremony. The association provided the vaccines because some Army personnel face increased exposure while carrying out duties in areas where dengue outbreaks are considered a high risk. The Army Medical Department noted that dengue can occur throughout the year. Although the Army already allocates funding and maintains prevention and control measures, military working environments can make it difficult for personnel to avoid Aedes mosquitoes , which transmit the disease. The donated vaccines will be distributed to Army personnel and officials in areas experiencing outbreaks, supporting existing public-health measures intended to reduce the risk of dengue among troops

supplementary_news.content_title: Clean water and waste management are key to fighting dengue
supplementary_news.content: Manila Bulletin Environment and Sustainability Clean water and waste management are key to fighting dengue Environment and Sustainability Clean water and waste management are key to fighting dengue By Henrylito D. Tacio Dengue is hyper-endemic in the Philippines. The World Health Organization (WHO) has observed cyclical increases in dengue cases, with significant outbreaks occurring every three to five years. The World Health Organization's warning signs for dengue. So, what does dengue have to do with the environment? Water, discarded plastic bottles, and poorly managed surroundings are part of the answer. Water serves a dual purpose in the context of dengue. Stagnant water facilitates mosquito reproduction, while adequate hydration is essential for patients recovering from the disease. According to the We Are Water Foundation, dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which deposit their eggs in clean, stagnant water found in artificial containers such as buckets, flower pots, and discarded items that collect rainwater. These breeding sites can be found around homes and communities. Poor water storage practices can increase the number of mosquito breeding sites and, consequently, the risk of dengue outbreaks. An Aedes mosquito, which can transmit dengue, rests on a surface. (Photo by Henrylito Tacio) Before the rainy season, the country also experiences intense heat. Many Filipinos store water in containers such as pails and barrels. When these containers are left uncovered and are not regularly emptied and cleaned, they can become breeding grounds for mosquitoes that transmit dengue. Managing outdoor water in shared spaces and routinely emptying or covering containers are important preventive measures to reduce mosquito populations. The same concern applies to discarded plastic waste. Plastic bottles, bags, sachets, food containers and wrappers can collect rainwater and become artificial catchments for stagnant water. Poorly managed plastic waste is particularly hazardous because even small containers can retain enough water for mosquito breeding. Discarded bottle caps and other small objects can also serve as breeding sites. Aedes mosquitoes are highly adapted to human environments and tend to stay close to people. The accumulation of plastic waste around residences, roadsides, and urban areas therefore creates numerous small water reservoirs where mosquitoes can breed. Poor waste management can also affect drainage systems. Discarded plastics can clog gutters and municipal drainage, resulting in localized flooding and stagnant water. This can create additional breeding sites throughout communities, particularly during the rainy season. The eggs of Aedes mosquitoes can also survive for months under dry conditions. When breeding sites are filled with water again, some eggs can hatch, allowing the mosquito population to increase. Children are among those most vulnerable to severe dengue. (Photo courtesy of Dr. Richard Mata) For people who contract dengue, adequate hydration is also important, particularly because the disease can cause fluid loss through fever, vomiting and plasma leakage. Water and oral rehydration solutions may help maintain fluid levels, while patients with severe dengue may require medical attention and intravenous fluids. The fight against dengue, therefore, is not only a health concern. It is also an environmental and community responsibility. Keeping surroundings clean, properly storing water, removing containers that can collect rainwater, and ensuring that drainage systems remain clear are simple measures, but they can reduce the places where mosquitoes breed. During the rainy season, dengue prevention efforts begin not only in hospitals and health centers but also in homes, streets, and communities. Preventing stagnant water and managing waste properly remain among the most practical ways to make the environment less favorable for dengue-carrying mosquitoes. close Manila Bulletin Weather Producer-20260819-09:03 CANCEL NEXT VIDEO play_arrow volume_mute AD % buffered 00:00 00:00 00:38 Powered by GliaStudios Related Tags Dengue waste management dengue cases Philippines

The Ministry of Health and Wellness is urging Belizeans to take action now by checking their homes, yards, workplaces, and communities for stagnant water, where the Aedes aegypti mosquito breeds. Health officials say dengue can range from mild illness to severe disease, and in some cases, it can be fatal. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, skin rash, bleeding, and difficulty breathing. The ministry is advising anyone experiencing symptoms to seek medical attention immediately. Residents are also being reminded to empty or cover containers that collect water, clear drains and yards, remove old tires, bottles and cans, use mosquito repellent, wear long sleeves when possible, and keep doors and windows properly screened. The ministry says dengue prevention is a shared responsibility and continues to work with communities and local authorities on surveillance and vector control. The state health and environment committee chairman said Johor recorded 7,965 cumulative dengue cases as of the 31st epidemiological week ending Aug 8, almost double the 4,037 cases recorded during the corresponding period last year. “Johor Baru and Kulai accounted for about 91% of the dengue cases in the state, largely due to their dense populations and concentration of housing estates and flats. “The situation is particularly concerning because the dominant dengue strain circulating now is associated with more severe infections and symptoms,” he said in an interview. Advertisement Powered by: 00:00 00:00 Ad will close in:10 seconds orclick to close He said the high number of infections was also placing additional pressure on the public healthcare system. In response to the situation, Ling said he chaired a special state dengue committee meeting last week, during which the Johor government approved an allocation of RM116,000 to the Health Department to support fogging operations. More than 90 large-scale gotong-royong programmes have also been planned, particularly in Johor Baru and Kulai, he said, adding that this was to raise awareness and encourage residents to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds. StarPicks How to compare the real cost of higher education “The worsening dengue situation requires urgent attention from the public as preventing the disease is a shared responsibility between the authorities and residents. “We want the people to make this a routine habit as it only takes about 10 minutes to inspect your home and surroundings to ensure there is no stagnant water in flower pots, containers, drains or puddles where mosquitoes can breed. Ling said the current weather pattern of hot and dry conditions combined with rainfall created ideal conditions for Aedes mosquitoes to reproduce, as they required only a small amount of standing water to breed. He urged those experiencing symptoms such as fever and fatigue to seek medical treatment immediately and request a dengue test from their doctor. “Early detection and treatment can help prevent complications and reduce the risk of severe dengue.” The latest figures mark a sharp deterioration from earlier in the year, when The Star reported in June that Johor had recorded a weekly high of 268 dengue cases, with Johor Baru accounting for 81% of infections. The Star also highlighted the emergence of DENV-3 as the dominant circulating serotype, with experts warning that a major shift could increase the risk of severe disease in some patients. Doctor explains Dengue fever is finally coming down, but why can this be the most dangerous phase of the illness? Doctor explains Aadya Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 16, 2026, 20:00 IST Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large Follow us 1/7 Doctor explains what is the most dangerous phase of Dengue fever A falling fever usually feels like good news. After several days of high temperature, body pain, weakness and poor appetite, seeing the thermometer return towards normal can bring a family a much-needed sense of relief. But dengue does not always follow that familiar pattern of illness getting better as the fever disappears. In fact, the period when the fever starts settling can be one of the most important points in the illness. This is when some patients enter the critical phase, a short window in which dengue can suddenly become serious. Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur, explained, “When dengue fever finally starts to fall, families often breathe a sigh of relief. But a drop in temperature does not always mean the danger is over. In fact, for some patients, this is when the critical phase of dengue can begin.” 2/7 The fever is falling, but something else may be changing Dengue usually moves through three broad phases: febrile, critical and recovery. The first is the febrile phase, when the patient has the familiar high fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, nausea or vomiting and sometimes a rash. Fever commonly lasts two to seven days. Then comes the part that can confuse families. The temperature may come down. The patient may even appear more comfortable. Yet, in some cases, the blood vessels are becoming more permeable. This can allow plasma, the liquid portion of blood, to move out of the bloodstream and into surrounding tissues. The process is known as plasma leakage. The problem is not simply that fluid has moved into another part of the body. Significant leakage can reduce the amount of fluid circulating inside the blood vessels. If the loss becomes substantial, blood pressure and circulation can fall, potentially causing dengue shock. That is why a normal-looking thermometer can sometimes give a false sense of security. 3/7 why does the danger appear when the fever goes away? The connection between falling fever and rising risk may sound strange, but it makes sense when dengue is viewed as a changing illness rather than simply a fever. During the febrile phase, the high temperature is often the symptom that gets the most attention. Once it drops, the family may assume the infection is ending. But around defervescence, the medical term for the period when fever settles, some patients enter the critical phase. The increased permeability of blood vessels can cause plasma leakage during this window. The CDC describes the critical phase as beginning at defervescence and typically lasting 24 to 48 hours. Most patients improve, but those who develop substantial plasma leakage can deteriorate within hours. This is also why the phrase “the fever has gone, so the dengue is gone” can be dangerous. The illness may still need close observation even though the most obvious symptom has disappeared. Dr Nair explained, “Dengue generally has three phases: febrile, critical, and recovery. The critical phase often happens around the time the fever goes down, usually between days 3 and 7 of illness, though the timing can vary. During this period, some patients can develop complications even after appearing to improve.” Most people with dengue do recover without developing severe disease. The concern is identifying the smaller group whose condition begins changing quickly. 4/7 Platelets matter, but they do not tell the whole story One of the most common things families watch during dengue is the platelet count. That number is important, but it should not become the only measure of whether a patient is safe. Platelets can fall during dengue, particularly around the critical phase. However, a low platelet count by itself does not automatically mean that a person has severe dengue. Similarly, a platelet count that has not fallen dramatically does not completely rule out a developing complication. Doctors look at the entire clinical picture. Blood pressure, pulse, urine output, hydration, fluid balance, haematocrit and changes in blood-test results can all provide important clues. A doctor may also look for evidence of fluid accumulation and assess how alert and comfortable the patient appears. There is a practical lesson here for families: do not judge recovery by one blood-test number. A patient with dengue is more than a platelet count on a report. 5/7 These are the signs that should never be brushed aside The hours after the fever settles deserve attention, particularly if the patient develops new symptoms instead of steadily improving. Dr Nair said, “The warning signs families should know are severe abdominal pain, ongoing vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, unusual drowsiness or restlessness, difficulty breathing, cold or clammy skin, and reduced urine output.” These are not symptoms to watch casually at home. Reduced urine output also matters because it can signal that the circulation and fluid balance are becoming abnormal. Difficulty breathing can occur when fluid accumulates around the lungs or when the patient's condition becomes more severe. A person who was eating, drinking and talking normally in the morning but becomes unusually sleepy, restless, breathless or cold later in the day needs medical assessment. Dengue can change quickly, so waiting for the next routine blood test may not always be appropriate. 6/7 What families should do when the fever starts falling The safest approach is not to panic when the fever drops, but also not to celebrate too early. The patient should continue following the treating doctor's advice during this period. Fluid intake, urine output, symptoms and overall behaviour need attention. Doctors may recommend repeat blood tests or clinical reviews depending on the patient's condition. Medication choices also matter. Dr Nair said, “Patients should also avoid self-medicating with aspirin or drugs like ibuprofen, which can increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol is usually preferred for fever, under proper medical advice.” It is also important not to assume that more fluids are always better. Dengue treatment requires careful attention to fluid balance. During the recovery phase, leaked fluid moves back into the bloodstream. Excessive or poorly timed fluid administration can therefore create problems, including fluid overload. The WHO dengue guideline specifically warns about this risk. Once the critical phase passes without major complications, the recovery phase generally begins. Appetite and overall well-being improve, urine output increases and the body's fluid balance gradually stabilises. Platelets may recover later than some other blood parameters, so improvement should again be judged as a whole rather than by one number. Dr Nair summed up the central message clearly: “The good news is that most dengue infections do not advance to severe dengue. Once the critical phase is over, patients enter recovery and typically start to improve.” So, when the fever falls, the thermometer should not be the only thing being checked. Watch the person, not just the number. A calmer patient with improving appetite, adequate urine output and no warning signs is reassuring. A patient whose fever has fallen but who develops severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulty, unusual drowsiness, cold skin or reduced urine output needs prompt medical attention. With dengue, the disappearance of fever can mark improvement. But for some patients, it can also mark the beginning of the most closely watched 24 to 48 hours of the illness. 7/7 Medical experts consulted This article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by: Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur. Inputs were used to explain why dengue can become more dangerous when the fever starts falling, what happens during the critical phase, and which warning signs require immediate medical attention. The patient should continue following the treating doctor's advice during this period. Fluid intake, urine output, symptoms and overall behaviour need attention. Doctors may recommend repeat blood tests or clinical reviews depending on the patient's condition. Medication choices also matter. Dr Nair said, “Patients should also avoid self-medicating with aspirin or drugs like ibuprofen, which can increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol is usually preferred for fever, under proper medical advice.” It is also important not to assume that more fluids are always better. Dengue treatment requires careful attention to fluid balance. During the recovery phase, leaked fluid moves back into the bloodstream. Excessive or poorly timed fluid administration can therefore create problems, including fluid overload. The WHO dengue guideline specifically warns about this risk. Once the critical phase passes without major complications, the recovery phase generally begins. Appetite and overall well-being improve, urine output increases and the body's fluid balance gradually stabilises. Platelets may recover later than some other blood parameters, so improvement should again be judged as a whole rather than by one number. Dr Nair summed up the central message clearly: “The good news is that most dengue infections do not advance to severe dengue. Once the critical phase is over, patients enter recovery and typically start to improve.” So, when the fever falls, the thermometer should not be the only thing being checked. Watch the person, not just the number. A calmer patient with improving appetite, adequate urine output and no warning signs is reassuring. A patient whose fever has fallen but who develops severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulty, unusual drowsiness, cold skin or reduced urine output needs prompt medical attention. With dengue, the disappearance of fever can mark improvement. But for some patients, it can also mark the beginning of the most closely watched 24 to 48 hours of the illness. 7/7 Medical experts consulted This article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by: Dr Ajay Nair, Sr. Consultant - Internal Medicine, Narayana Hospital, Jaipur. Inputs were used to explain why dengue can become more dangerous when the fever starts falling, what happens during the critical phase, and which warning signs require immediate medical attention. 什么是登革热 “登革”一词,来源于西班牙语“dengue”。直到1869年伦敦皇家内科学院将此病定名为“登革热”,一直沿用至今。 登革热(Dengue fever)是由登革病毒(Dengue virus,DENV)经蚊媒传播引起的急性虫媒传染病。它的传播速度快,发病率高,是目前世界上分布最广、发病人数最多、危害最大的重要虫媒病毒传染病之一,在我国属于乙类传染病。 我国登革热高发季节为夏秋季,一般自每年5月开始逐渐增多,8—10月为发病高峰期。 登革热的传播和症状特点如何 登革病毒存在于登革热感染者或隐性感染者的血液中,主要经白纹伊蚊和埃及伊蚊(俗称“花蚊子”)传播。雌性伊蚊叮咬携带病毒的感染者后,病毒就会在蚊子体内大量复制,伊蚊再叮咬其他人时病毒就会被传播。传播途径主要是“感染者→伊蚊→其他人”,一般不会在人与人之间直接传播。 人体感染登革病毒后,潜伏期一般为1~14天,多为5~9天。 登革热的典型症状如下: 1.热 首发症状多为突发高热(40°C以上)伴畏寒,通常持续5~8天。 2.痛 头痛、眼眶痛、肌肉和骨关节剧烈酸痛。 3.红 面、颈、胸部潮红。 4.疹 分布于头面部或四肢躯干,为充血性皮疹或点状出血疹。 5.其他 腹痛腹泻等胃肠道症状;皮下或黏膜出血、牙龈出血、鼻衄等;白细胞计数和血小板减少;严重者甚至出现休克或多脏器功能损伤。 可通过体格检查、实验室检查(血常规、血清学检查)和影像学检查(CT、B超、磁共振),结合流行病学史和临床表现来判断和诊断。 旅游出行如何防控 1.在外应穿着长袖衣服及长裤,并使用驱蚊液,预防蚊子叮咬。 2.酒店、民宿房间应关好纱门、纱窗,房间可以使用蚊香、灭蚊气雾剂等,尤其要注意婴儿床和婴儿车,也要装置蚊帐。 3.在家中使用杀虫剂灭蚊时,要按照产品的说明进行操作,避免儿童接触。 4.避免在树阴、草丛、凉亭等户外阴暗处逗留。 5.如果出现发烧、皮疹等疑似症状,应及时就诊并主动说明被叮咬的情况。 家居日常如何防控 1.家里安装纱门纱窗和使用蚊帐,适时使用防蚊液、蚊香、电蚊拍、杀虫喷雾剂等进行驱蚊。 2.避免在蚊虫出没频繁的时段(上午7—9点和下午4—6点)在树阴、草丛、凉亭等户外阴暗处逗留,出门穿着浅色长袖衣服及长裤。 3.定期清除家居环境积水,及时清理饮料罐、食品盒、玻璃瓶等小容器垃圾,排清可能孳生蚊虫的积水。 登革热作为一种气候敏感的虫媒传染病具有明显的季节性,它属于自限性疾病,1~2周左右可恢复,并发症不常见,病死率较低,一般无后遗症。做好防蚊措施,避免蚊虫叮咬是预防登革热的最佳方式。 来源丨广东疾控微信公众号 一审丨萧渝桦 二审丨罗燕英 三审丨林伟志 创文: 觉得不错,请点这里↓↓↓ 特别声明:以上内容(如有图片或视频亦包括在内)为自媒体平台“网易号”用户上传并发布,本平台仅提供信息存储服务。 Notice: The content above (including the pictures and videos if any) is uploaded and posted by a user of NetEase Hao, which is a social media platform and only provides information storage services. 关闭 注册|手机发跟贴 登录并发贴 网友评论仅供其表达个人看法,并不表明网易立场。 目前没有热门跟贴 目前没有跟贴,欢迎你发表观点 查看更多跟贴 去跟贴广场看看 /阅读下一篇/ 返回网易首页 下载网易新闻客户端 相关推荐 热点推荐 速看!预防基孔肯雅热和登革热,从夏季防蚊开始 龙川发布 2026-08-19 14:55:29 0 跟贴 0 柳城县多措并举做好这项工作 柳城人柳城事 2026-08-19 17:03:47 0 跟贴 0 东莞体彩开展虫媒传染病防控专项排查整治 新快报新闻 2026-08-19 08:25:26 1 跟贴 1 存在多项重大事故隐患 中央考核巡查组在内蒙古多地明查暗访 央视新闻客户端 2026-08-19 13:47:00 23 跟贴 23 北京多措并举织密夏季防蚊“防护网” 北青网-北京青年报 2026-08-19 09:44:02 0 跟贴 0 北京千余家社区、公园和单位参与“无蚊害社区”建设 新京报 2026-08-19 13:25:07 1 跟贴 1 “最近几乎每天都有”!北京多区接警量翻倍,一旦直接接触立即就医!
